title: Number Systems
prerequisites: Familiarity with natural numbers, whole numbers and integers.
Ability to convert a fraction into a decimal.
Basic knowledge of squares, square roots and the number line.
Understanding of laws of exponents for integer powers.

topics.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers
topics.quick_summary: A rational number can be written as p/q with q ≠ 0 and has a terminating or repeating decimal, while an irrational number cannot and has a non-terminating non-repeating decimal.
topics.real_life: The ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter is π, a number no fraction can ever express exactly — which is why we always approximate it.

detailed.definition: A rational number is one that can be expressed in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. An irrational number cannot be expressed in this form. Together they form the real numbers.
detailed.key_idea: The decimal expansion is the practical test. Terminating or recurring means rational; non-terminating and non-recurring means irrational. Every real number is one or the other, never both.
detailed.working_principle: A rational number p/q in lowest terms has a terminating decimal exactly when the denominator's prime factors are only 2s and 5s. Otherwise the decimal recurs.
applications: √2, √3, √5, π and e are irrational; 0.101001000100001... is irrational by construction.
There are infinitely many rational and irrational numbers between any two distinct real numbers.
√2 can be located on the number line using the Pythagoras theorem on a unit square.

points: Rational: terminating or non-terminating recurring decimal.
p/q terminates only if the denominator in lowest terms is of the form 2ᵐ5ⁿ.
Sum or product of a rational and an irrational number is always irrational.
The sum or product of two irrational numbers may be rational, e.g. √2 × √2 = 2.
mistakes: Calling 22/7 irrational; it is rational and only an approximation to π.
Assuming the sum of two irrational numbers must be irrational — (2 + √3) + (2 − √3) = 4.
Writing √4 as irrational; it equals 2 and is rational.
topics.memory_hook: 'Repeats or Ends = Rational; Rambles forever = Irrational.'
topics.advanced: Irrational numbers vastly outnumber rational ones: the rationals are countable while the reals are not. If you could pick a real number at random, the probability of getting a rational is exactly zero.

formulas.name: Rationalising the Denominator
formulas.variables: a = rational part, √b = irrational part of the denominator.
formulas.when_to_use: Whenever a surd appears in a denominator and must be removed.
formulas.common_mistakes: Changing the sign of the wrong term, or forgetting to multiply the numerator as well.
formulas.shortcut: Multiply by the conjugate — change the sign between the two terms.

topics.title: Laws of Exponents and Surds
topics.quick_summary: The laws of exponents extend from integer to rational powers, allowing roots to be written as fractional indices and simplified using the same rules.
topics.real_life: Compound interest, population growth and sound intensity are all computed with exponent laws, which is why they are worth complete fluency.

detailed.definition: For a positive real number a and rational numbers m and n, aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. A surd is an irrational root of a rational number, such as √2 or ∛5.
detailed.key_idea: Writing a root as a fractional index — ⁿ√a = a^(1/n) — turns every root manipulation into an exponent manipulation, so one set of rules covers both.
detailed.working_principle: Surds are simplified by extracting perfect squares (or cubes) from under the radical, and like surds are added or subtracted just as like terms are.
applications: a^(m/n) = ⁿ√(aᵐ) connects indices and roots directly.

points: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0.
Only like surds can be added or subtracted.
The laws hold for a > 0; for negative bases with fractional powers they can fail.
mistakes: Writing (a + b)ⁿ = aⁿ + bⁿ, which is false.
Adding unlike surds, e.g. treating √2 + √3 as √5.
Forgetting that a⁰ = 1 only when a ≠ 0.
topics.memory_hook: 'Multiply → add powers; Divide → subtract powers; Power of a power → multiply.'
topics.advanced: Defining a^x for irrational x requires limits, which is where exponents connect to calculus. This is why the natural exponential e^x, defined by its own derivative, becomes the base of choice in higher mathematics.

formulas.name: Laws of Exponents
formulas.formula: aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ,  aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ,  (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ,  a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ
formulas.variables: a = base (a > 0), m and n = rational exponents.
formulas.when_to_use: For all simplification of powers, roots and surds.
formulas.common_mistakes: Adding the exponents when raising a power to a power instead of multiplying them.
formulas.shortcut: Same base multiplied → add; same base divided → subtract.

formulas.name: Fractional Exponent
formulas.variables: a = positive base, m = power, n = root index.
formulas.when_to_use: To convert between root notation and index notation.
formulas.common_mistakes: Interchanging the roles of m and n.
formulas.shortcut: The denominator of the fraction is the root; the numerator is the power.
